item.title: How Firms Can Profit by Becoming Less Competitive
item.description:
Background

Firms usually try to become more competitive by expanding capacity, reaching more customers, and lowering costs. When a business closes a plant or leaves a profitable market, we tend to assume that something has gone wrong.

This paper examines theoretically whether deliberately becoming less competitive can encourage industry consolidation through rival mergers and ultimately increase a firm’s own profit.

item.title: Firm Entry under Coopetition
item.description:
Background

A new competitor is usually unwelcome news for an existing business. More firms compete for the same customers, making it harder for each to earn a profit.

But firms sometimes help cultivate the market in which they compete. Hotels and restaurants promote a tourist destination; producers advertise a product category; businesses contribute to shared infrastructure that attracts customers. In these settings, a new entrant is both an additional rival and an additional contributor to the market’s development.
